community-s8h1/u1.input: My research for this article turned up no well-documented case of a child in an intentional community who remained seriously dangerous to other people, with the whole sequence on record: the conduct, the assessment, the intervention, the review, and what happened later. Maybe the records are private, or the cases went elsewhere. Either way, I can't claim communities already know how to handle the hardest version on their own. The child, the family, and the people at risk all need access to competent help and review that the home community doesn't control.
community-s8h1/u1.A: During my research on this subject I failed to turn up any good accounts, inside an intentional community, of what was done for children who were dangerous to others. Perhaps this is because such cases were handled privately, or were handled outside the community. In any case, until it can be shown that such cases can be handled within a community, it is important to have access to competent help and review outside the control of the community in which the child, her family, and potential victims live.
community-s8h1/u1.B: As I mention in the article , despite searching for examples I couldn't find a well-documented example of an intentional community dealing with a child who was dangerous to other people, where the whole process was described and the child was still dangerous at the end. It's possible that this has happened but that the details are kept secret, or that such children are always dealt with outside the community. But regardless, I think it's necessary to have access to competent assistance and review which the community itself does not control.

community-s8h1/u2.input: They'll also need transferable skills and education, relationships outside the community, access to their own records and documents, and at least one plausible next step, whether that's school, an apprenticeship, work, family or another community. It's great if the community has the resources to help with the transition, with temporary housing, travel, tools or a little money set aside, but even if it doesn't, it can still not punish anyone for leaving, and not hold back the knowledge and records a young adult needs to function out there. No upbringing gives you perfect freedom, and the point isn't to erase path dependence. It's to not turn belonging into a trap.
community-s8h1/u2.A: This would include some skills or education that can be transferred outside the community, some relationships with people outside the community, some records and documents that they can take with them, at least one idea of what to do next (school, apprenticeship, job, family, community, etc), and ideally some community resources available to help transition, provide temporary housing, pay for travel, provide tools or money, etc. If that's too much, at least not penalizing people for leaving and not preventing them from taking knowledge and records with them would be better than nothing. This doesn't have to be perfect, just better than the extreme path dependence most people have.
community-s8h1/u2.B: It's also important that they be taught skills and education that will let them succeed outside the community, that they be allowed to form relationships outside the community, that they be given access to their own records and documents, and that they be given some reasonable choices for what to do next (school, apprenticeship, work, family, community, etc.) when they leave. It's also good, though perhaps harder, for the community to help the kids transition out, whether by providing temporary housing, travel, tools, money, etc. It the community is unwilling to do any of these things, at the very least it should not make it costly to leave, and should not inhibit the kids from getting the information and records they need when they do leave. No community can fully negate path dependence, but they can at least not make things worse.

community-s8h1/u3.input:
Couples who share a home, a culture and a bed still split over screens, vaccines, schooling, religion, food, discipline and medical care. Multiply that by twenty adults, each with their own childhood.

Goodwill doesn't answer those questions once a child is already living inside the disagreement. There has to be enough common ground on how kids are raised that the community hangs together. And the parents still need room to be parents.
community-s8h1/u3.A:
It’s amazing to see how couples living together, of the same culture and background, let alone sharing the same bed, can have such different opinions about screens, vaccinations, school, religion, food, discipline, medical care, etc., etc. And that’s just two people. Now think of 20 adults, all with different childhood experiences.

In a community like this, it’s not enough to say “well, at least everyone means well.” There has to be a substantial area of agreement about how to raise children – otherwise, what reason do people have to stay in the community? At the same time, parents have to feel like they can be parents.
community-s8h1/u3.B:
People who live together, share the same culture and sleep in the same bed can disagree on screen time, vaccines, schooling, religion, what they eat, how they are disciplined and medical care, to name a few. That is two people - imagine twenty adults together with their own childhood influences.

It is not enough to just have a desire to make it work - there has to be some common ground about how children are raised if the community is going to survive - while still allowing parents to parent.

Even couples living together, sharing the same culture, sharing the same bed, split on issues like screen time, vacciantions, schooling, religion, what food to eat, how to discipline the kids, what medical treatments to allow, etc. Those are just a few that come to mind. Imagine 20 people with different childhoods.

Good will only goes so far if the kids are already there. There needs to be a lot of agreement on how to raise kids if the community is to stay together. The parents have to be allowed to parent.
community-s8h1/u4.B:
But many will split off, become their own thing with their own values rather than wait till their kids inherit the original, and that may feel like loss to the parents.

People who live together, share a culture, sometimes even a bed, nevertheless split over whose turn it is to look at the screen, whether to vaccinate or not, whether to send kids to school, what religion to practice, what to eat, how to punish kids, how to handle medical issues, etc, etc. Multiply that by twenty people with twenty different pasts.

Good will is great, but in the end there has to be a LOT of agreement about how to raise kids for parents to feel like they can be parents in such a community.
